questions.prompt: Why does BITS make attacker network activity harder to attribute?
options: It encrypts all traffic with a custom protocol
The transfer is performed by a service process rather than the malware's own, so connections are attributed to svchost.exe doing something routine
It routes traffic through Microsoft servers
questions.explanation: Because BITS performs the transfer on the caller's behalf, the outbound connection looks like ordinary Windows update activity rather than a process making its own request.

questions.prompt: Which bitsadmin option converts a download job into a persistence mechanism?
options: /SetNotifyCmdLine, which runs a specified command when the job completes or errors
questions.explanation: The notification command line turns job completion or failure into an execution trigger -- and because jobs have a 90-day default lifetime, a job that keeps failing keeps firing it.

questions.prompt: Why does a triage checking registry autoruns and scheduled tasks miss BITS persistence entirely?
options: BITS jobs are stored in the Security event log only
BITS jobs live in a queue database under C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Network\Downloader\, which is neither a registry key nor a scheduled task
BITS jobs exist only in memory
BITS jobs are stored in the WMI repository
questions.explanation: The queue database (qmgr.db on modern Windows) is a distinct storage location that standard autorun-focused triage does not cover.

questions.prompt: Why does the /allusers flag matter when enumerating BITS jobs?
options: It shows completed jobs as well as active ones
A job created by another user is invisible without it
questions.explanation: Without /allusers, enumeration only returns jobs owned by the current user -- so an attacker's job created under a different account simply will not appear.
